prompt: RSI (rapid sequence intubation) conceptually includes:

options.text: Near-simultaneous sedation and neuromuscular blockade to facilitate intubation in at-risk patients
Paralysis first, then a sedative once tube placement is confirmed so induction does not drop the BP
Awake intubation with topical anesthesia and light sedation, avoiding a paralytic so breathing continues
Sedation alone titrated to tolerate laryngoscopy, with the paralytic held back for a failed first attempt

explanation: RSI requires preparation, preoxygenation, drugs, and post-intubation management; follows local ALS protocols/scope.

distractorExplanations.b: Reverses the RSI sequence: a paralytic given before the induction agent leaves the patient awake and paralyzed.
distractorExplanations.c: Describes an awake/topicalized intubation technique; RSI by definition pairs an induction agent with a paralytic.
distractorExplanations.d: That is sedation-facilitated intubation; RSI gives the paralytic immediately after induction, not as a rescue drug.

prompt: Endotracheal tube placement confirmation should include

options.text: Direct visualization of the tube passing the cords, with capnography reserved for difficult intubations
Waveform capnography plus clinical assessments (bilateral breath sounds, chest rise)
A colorimetric ETCO2 detector alone, which also tracks tube position continuously during transport
Pulse oximetry rising within 30 seconds plus breath sounds, which reliably excludes esophageal placement

explanation: Continuous waveform ETCO2 is the gold standard adjunct for confirming/monitoring ETT position.

distractorExplanations.a: Seeing the tube pass the cords can be wrong or the tube can move; waveform capnography is expected for every intubation.
distractorExplanations.c: Colorimetric detectors give a one-time color change and cannot monitor continuously; dislodgement en route would be missed.
distractorExplanations.d: SpO2 lags for minutes after preoxygenation, so a normal reading does not exclude an esophageal tube; capnography does.

prompt: A surgical cricothyrotomy is indicated when:

options.text: Two failed intubation attempts while SpO2 stays above 94% with BVM ventilation
Severe facial trauma in a child under 10 years old who needs a definitive airway
Cannot intubate/cannot oxygenate scenarios require a front-of-neck airway
Status asthmaticus with poor air movement, before any attempt at BVM or intubation

explanation: Cric is a rescue airway for failed airway algorithms—not routine first-line.

distractorExplanations.a: If BVM still oxygenates (SpO2 above 94%), this is cannot-intubate-CAN-oxygenate: use an SGA/BVM, not a surgical cric.
distractorExplanations.b: Surgical cricothyrotomy is generally contraindicated in young children (small cricothyroid membrane); needle cric is used.
distractorExplanations.d: Wrong timing: front-of-neck access is the last step of the failed-airway algorithm, never a first move in asthma.

options.text: Decreasing oxygen saturation intentionally
Replacing the need for FiO2
Guaranteeing no pneumothorax risk
Preventing alveolar collapse and improving oxygenation

explanation: PEEP improves FRC/oxygenation but can reduce venous return and risk barotrauma.

distractorExplanations.a: PEEP should improve oxygenation.
distractorExplanations.b: FiO2 still titrated.
distractorExplanations.c: Pneumothorax risk can rise with high pressures.

prompt: Needle thoracostomy for tension pneumothorax is classically placed

options.text: 2nd intercostal space midclavicular line or 4th/5th ICS mid/anterior axillary
2nd ICS midclavicular line, inserting the needle along the inferior border of the 2nd rib
5th intercostal space at the midclavicular line, directly over the nipple on the affected side
Subxiphoid, angled toward the left shoulder, the same approach used for pericardiocentesis

explanation: Know both traditional MCL and lateral sites—follow current service protocol.

distractorExplanations.b: Needle goes over the superior border of the 3rd rib; the intercostal artery, vein, and nerve run under each rib.
distractorExplanations.c: The 5th ICS midclavicular site lies over the heart on the left; lateral sites use the mid/anterior axillary line.
distractorExplanations.d: Subxiphoid toward the left shoulder is the pericardiocentesis landmark for tamponade, not pleural decompression.

prompt: Waveform capnography in cardiac arrest can help

options.text: Confirm ROSC when ETCO2 drops suddenly below 10 mm Hg during compressions
Indicate CPR quality and early ROSC (sudden ETCO2 rise)
Decide on shocks by showing whether the rhythm is VF or pulseless VT
Titrate ventilations upward until ETCO2 falls below 20 mm Hg

explanation: Low ETCO2 suggests poor pulmonary blood flow/CPR; sustained rise may signal ROSC.

distractorExplanations.a: Direction is reversed: ROSC shows as an abrupt ETCO2 rise (often to 35–45); a fall below 10 signals poor CPR.
distractorExplanations.c: Rhythm and shock decisions come from the ECG/monitor; capnography reflects perfusion and ventilation, not rhythm.
distractorExplanations.d: Hyperventilating to a low ETCO2 raises intrathoracic pressure and cuts coronary perfusion; ETCO2 under 10 means weak CPR.

prompt: Apneic oxygenation during RSI often uses

options.text: A non-rebreather mask kept on the face at 15 L/min during laryngoscopy
Rapid BVM ventilation at 20+ breaths/min between paralysis and laryngoscopy
High-flow nasal oxygen during apnea to prolong safe apnea time
Holding all oxygen until the tube is placed, to avoid absorption atelectasis

explanation: Passive oxygenation via NC can delay desaturation during laryngoscopy.

distractorExplanations.a: A face mask has to come off for laryngoscopy, so it cannot deliver oxygen during apnea; a nasal cannula stays on.
distractorExplanations.b: Aggressive bagging after paralysis insufflates the stomach and raises aspiration risk; apneic oxygenation is passive.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a minor theoretical concern with practice; withholding oxygen shortens safe apnea time and speeds desaturation.

prompt: Laryngospasm management may include

options.text: Immediate blind finger sweeps and back blows, as for a foreign-body obstruction
Nebulized racemic epinephrine first-line, the same treatment used for croup stridor
Immediate needle cricothyrotomy before any attempt at positive-pressure ventilation
High-quality BVM with jaw thrust/CPAP pressure and progressive advanced measures

explanation: Break spasm with airway maneuvers/pressure; drugs/paralysis per advanced protocols if needed.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats laryngospasm like a choking FBAO; blind sweeps are not recommended and back blows do not open closed cords.
distractorExplanations.b: Racemic epinephrine treats subglottic edema in croup; laryngospasm is reflex cord closure broken by pressure/jaw thrust.
distractorExplanations.c: Skips the sequence: most laryngospasm resolves with jaw thrust and CPAP/BVM pressure; surgical access is the last resort.

prompt: The Mallampati classification estimates

options.text: Relative difficulty of laryngoscopy based on oropharyngeal structures visible
Glottic view during direct laryngoscopy, graded from full cords to epiglottis only
Thyromental distance as a predictor of difficult bag-mask ventilation
Risk of difficult BVM from beard, obesity, age, and no teeth (MOANS)

explanation: Higher Mallampati scores correlate with potentially difficult airways—still imperfect.

distractorExplanations.b: That is the Cormack-Lehane grade, seen during laryngoscopy; Mallampati is assessed beforehand with the mouth open.
distractorExplanations.c: Thyromental distance is part of the LEMON 3-3-2 evaluation, and Mallampati predicts laryngoscopy, not BVM difficulty.
distractorExplanations.d: MOANS is the mnemonic for difficult bag-mask ventilation; Mallampati grades visible oropharyngeal structures.

prompt: Failed airway algorithm priority is

options.text: Securing a definitive tube on the next attempt before switching to rescue devices
Oxygenation/ventilation—rescue devices and front-of-neck access if needed
Immediate surgical cricothyrotomy after the first failed attempt, even if BVM works
Passing a bougie blindly on repeated attempts until SpO2 falls below 80%

explanation: Limit attempts; maximize oxygenation with SGA/BVM/cric as indicated.

distractorExplanations.a: Prioritizes the tube over oxygen; repeated attempts cause edema and hypoxia, so failed airways move to SGA/BVM first.
distractorExplanations.c: If BVM or an SGA oxygenates, the patient is not CICO; front-of-neck access is reserved for cannot-oxygenate situations.
distractorExplanations.d: Waiting for SpO2 to fall before stopping attempts is backwards; attempts are limited and oxygenation is restored first.

prompt: RSI (rapid sequence intubation) preparation should always include

options.text: Suction set up after the first attempt, since secretions are rarely present in fasting patients
A single preferred blade size, with backup devices left in the ambulance to keep the scene uncluttered
Equipment readiness for failed airway (BVM, suction, extraglottic/surgical backup) and confirmation plan
Preoxygenation for 30 seconds by BVM at 30 breaths/min, followed directly by laryngoscopy

explanation: Airway attempts need oxygenation strategy and failure pathway ready.

distractorExplanations.b: Backups stored in the ambulance are not ready; failed-airway gear (SGA, other blade, cric kit) must be at the head.
distractorExplanations.d: Preoxygenation takes about 3 minutes (or 8 vital-capacity breaths), not 30 seconds of rapid bagging into the stomach.

prompt: Waveform capnography after intubation primarily helps confirm

options.text: Arterial oxygen saturation, replacing the need for a pulse oximeter after intubation
Correct tube depth, showing whether the tip sits above the carina or in a mainstem bronchus
Exact PaCO2, since ETCO2 equals arterial CO2 in shock and cardiac arrest
Tracheal placement and ongoing ventilation effectiveness/CO2 elimination

explanation: Persistent ETCO2 waveform supports tracheal tube placement and monitors ventilation.

distractorExplanations.a: Capnography measures exhaled CO2, not oxygenation; SpO2 monitoring is still required after intubation.
distractorExplanations.b: A right mainstem tube still produces a normal waveform; depth is checked by breath sounds, tube marking, and imaging.
distractorExplanations.c: ETCO2 underestimates PaCO2, and the gap widens in shock and arrest because of reduced pulmonary blood flow.

prompt: A patient with status asthmaticus may benefit from which ventilation concept?

options.text: Allowing adequate expiratory time and avoiding excessive rates that cause auto-PEEP
Rates of 20–24 breaths/min with large tidal volumes to blow off retained CO2
A short expiratory time with a 1:1 I:E ratio to keep minute ventilation high
Permissive hypoxia, keeping SpO2 near 85% to protect the hypoxic drive

explanation: Obstructive disease needs time to exhale; stacked breaths cause hypotension/pneumothorax risk.

distractorExplanations.b: Fast rates and big volumes shorten exhalation and stack breaths, causing auto-PEEP, hypotension, and pneumothorax.
distractorExplanations.c: Obstructive disease needs a long exhalation (I:E of 1:4 or more); a 1:1 ratio traps air with every breath.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the COPD hypoxic-drive teaching with asthma; status asthmaticus needs oxygen, and the tolerated value is CO2.

prompt: Needle cricothyrotomy/surgical airway is considered when:

options.text: Intubation fails twice but an SGA gives good chest rise
You cannot oxygenate/ventilate and cannot intubate (CICO)
A child with epiglottitis is drooling but holds SpO2 at 95%
As the first step for a snoring airway before a jaw thrust

explanation: Front-of-neck access is a last-resort failed airway intervention.

distractorExplanations.a: An SGA that ventilates means the patient can be oxygenated; continue with the SGA rather than cutting the neck.
distractorExplanations.c: A child who is oxygenating should be kept calm and transported; instrumenting the airway can trigger full obstruction.
distractorExplanations.d: Snoring is partial upper-airway obstruction fixed by positioning, jaw thrust, and adjuncts long before surgical access.

prompt: Positive-pressure ventilation in a hypotensive patient can worsen BP because it

options.text: Increases preload by pushing blood from the lungs into the left atrium
Causes vasodilation through hyperoxia-induced nitric oxide release
Increases intrathoracic pressure and may reduce venous return
Triggers a vagal reflex that slows the heart below 50 beats/min

explanation: Excessive ventilation/PPv can drop preload—use appropriate rates/volumes and treat shock.

distractorExplanations.a: Positive pressure lowers venous return to the right heart, so overall preload falls rather than rises.
distractorExplanations.b: Hyperoxia tends to cause vasoconstriction; the BP drop comes from raised intrathoracic pressure reducing venous return.
distractorExplanations.d: PPV-related hypotension is a preload problem from intrathoracic pressure, not a vagal bradycardia reflex.

prompt: STEMI recognition on 12-lead focuses on

options.text: ST elevation meeting criteria in anatomically contiguous leads
Diffuse ST elevation in nearly all leads with PR depression
Peaked T waves alone in the precordial leads with a flat ST
ST elevation in two non-contiguous leads such as II and V2

explanation: Know anterior/inferior/lateral distributions; LBBB/paced rhythms complicate interpretation.

distractorExplanations.b: Diffuse ST elevation with PR depression is the classic pericarditis pattern, not a regional STEMI territory.
distractorExplanations.c: Peaked T waves without ST elevation suggest hyperkalemia or a hyperacute phase and do not meet STEMI criteria.
distractorExplanations.d: STEMI criteria require elevation in contiguous leads of one territory; II (inferior) and V2 (septal) are not contiguous.

prompt: For adult VF/pVT, defibrillation energy should be

options.text: 2 J/kg biphasic for adults, escalating to 4 J/kg on the second and later shocks
Per manufacturer biphasic recommended dose (often 120–200 J) then resume CPR
360 J synchronized, then a pulse check before resuming CPR
50–100 J biphasic, the dose used for narrow regular tachycardia

explanation: VF/pVT = unsynchronized defibrillation; synchronized cardioversion is for unstable tachycardias with pulse.

distractorExplanations.a: 2 J/kg then 4 J/kg is the pediatric defibrillation dosing; adults use the manufacturer dose, typically 120–200 J biphasic.
distractorExplanations.c: VF has no QRS to synchronize to, and CPR resumes immediately after the shock without a pulse check.
distractorExplanations.d: 50–100 J is a synchronized cardioversion starting dose for narrow regular tachycardia, too low for VF/pVT.

prompt: Atropine for symptomatic bradycardia adult dose commonly taught is

options.text: 0.02 mg/kg IV, minimum 0.1 mg, maximum single dose 0.5 mg
0.5 mg IV every 3–5 minutes up to 3 mg
1 mg IV every 3–5 minutes up to 3 mg
3 mg IV once as a single full vagolytic dose

explanation: If atropine fails, TCP/dopamine/epinephrine infusions per algorithm. Current AHA protocols use the 1 mg dose.

distractorExplanations.a: That is the pediatric atropine dose; adult symptomatic bradycardia uses 1 mg every 3–5 minutes up to 3 mg.
distractorExplanations.b: 0.5 mg was the pre-2020 AHA adult dose; current guidelines raised the bradycardia dose to 1 mg (maximum 3 mg).
distractorExplanations.d: A single 3 mg push was older asystole dosing; bradycardia is treated with repeated 1 mg doses to a 3 mg total.

prompt: Adenosine is indicated for:

options.text: Irregular narrow-complex atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular rate
Stable irregular wide-complex tachycardia that may be pre-excited AF
Symptomatic sinus bradycardia that has not responded to atropine
Stable regular narrow-complex SVT after vagal maneuvers

explanation: Adenosine briefly blocks AV node; caution in irregular wide-complex differentials.

distractorExplanations.a: AF is irregular and not AV-node re-entrant; adenosine only briefly slows it and does not convert it.
distractorExplanations.b: Adenosine in irregular wide-complex (possible pre-excited AF) can speed accessory-pathway conduction into VF.
distractorExplanations.c: Adenosine blocks the AV node and would worsen bradycardia; atropine failure moves to pacing or epi/dopamine drips.

prompt: ROSC care includes:

options.text: Airway optimization, BP support, 12-lead, and temperature/neuro considerations
Ventilating at 20–30 breaths/min to bring ETCO2 down to 20 mm Hg quickly
Titrating oxygen to SpO2 of 100% and keeping SBP near 80 mm Hg to protect the heart
Removing the pads once a pulse returns and transporting without a 12-lead to save time

explanation: Avoid hyperventilation; support perfusion and identify cause (H's/T's). Post-ROSC care includes targeted temperature management and neuro assessment.

distractorExplanations.b: Post-ROSC ventilation targets about 10/min and ETCO2 35–45; hyperventilation causes cerebral vasoconstriction.
distractorExplanations.c: ROSC targets are SpO2 92–98% (avoid hyperoxia) and SBP at least 90 / MAP at least 65, not permissive hypotension.
distractorExplanations.d: Rearrest is common after ROSC; pads stay on, monitoring continues, and a 12-lead screens for STEMI and PCI.

prompt: Right ventricular infarction accompanying inferior MI suggests caution with:

options.text: Aspirin, because RV infarction carries a higher bleeding risk
Nitroglycerin/preload reducers due to preload dependence
Small IV fluid boluses, since the RV is already volume overloaded
Lying the patient flat, since it lowers right-sided filling pressure

explanation: RV MI patients may become profoundly hypotensive with nitro; fluid support often needed.

distractorExplanations.a: Aspirin is still given in RV infarction; there is no added bleeding risk, and the caution is about preload reduction.
distractorExplanations.c: The infarcted RV is preload-dependent, so fluid boluses are the treatment for hypotension, not the thing to avoid.
distractorExplanations.d: Lying flat increases venous return and helps a preload-dependent RV; the real danger is nitrates and diuretics.

prompt: Wide-complex regular tachycardia in an unstable patient is treated with:

options.text: Adenosine 6 mg rapid IV push first, then cardioversion if it fails
Amiodarone 150 mg IV over 10 minutes, repeated as needed, before any electrical therapy
Prompt synchronized cardioversion (or defibrillation if pulseless/degenerate)
Transcutaneous pacing at a rate above the tachycardia to overdrive it

explanation: Unstable = shock; stable wide-complex needs expert interpretation/antiarrhythmics per protocol.

distractorExplanations.a: Adenosine is considered only for stable regular monomorphic wide-complex rhythms; unstable patients get shocked now.
distractorExplanations.b: Amiodarone 150 mg over 10 minutes is the stable wide-complex tachycardia option; instability calls for cardioversion.
distractorExplanations.d: Overdrive pacing is a specialist in-hospital technique; prehospital unstable VT is treated with synchronized shocks.

prompt: Amiodarone in cardiac arrest (VF/pVT refractory) adult dosing commonly taught includes:

options.text: 1–1.5 mg/kg IV/IO first dose, then 0.5–0.75 mg/kg
5 mg/kg IV/IO first dose, repeated up to twice
150 mg IV over 10 minutes, then 1 mg/min
300 mg IV/IO first dose, then 150 mg

explanation: Follow current ACLS drug sequence with CPR/defibrillation priority.

distractorExplanations.a: That is the lidocaine dosing for refractory VF/pVT, the alternative antiarrhythmic, not amiodarone.
distractorExplanations.b: 5 mg/kg repeated up to a 15 mg/kg total is the pediatric amiodarone dose; adults get 300 mg then 150 mg.
distractorExplanations.c: 150 mg over 10 minutes is the stable VT dose with a pulse; arrest dosing is a 300 mg push then 150 mg.

prompt: CPAP for acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema helps by:

options.text: Increasing intrathoracic pressure to reduce preload/afterload and improve oxygenation
Raising preload so the failing left ventricle can stretch and pump harder
Removing alveolar fluid by increasing renal sodium excretion within minutes
Reducing the work of breathing by lowering intrathoracic pressure on inhalation

explanation: CPAP is a key ALS tool for CHF/flash edema when patient can cooperate.

distractorExplanations.b: CPAP lowers venous return (preload) to the overloaded heart; adding preload would worsen pulmonary edema.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses CPAP with diuretic action; CPAP pushes fluid back and recruits alveoli mechanically, with no renal effect.
distractorExplanations.d: CPAP raises intrathoracic pressure through the whole breath; that rise is what cuts preload and afterload.

prompt: Hyperkalemia ECG changes may include

options.text: Flattened T waves, ST depression, and prominent U waves
Peaked T waves, widened QRS, and sine-wave progression
Prolonged QT with notched T waves and torsades risk
Osborn J waves at the QRS-ST junction with bradycardia

explanation: Severe hyperK is a life threat treated with calcium/stabilizers/shifting agents per protocol.

distractorExplanations.c: A long QT with torsades risk points to hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, or drugs, not to high potassium.
distractorExplanations.d: Osborn (J) waves are the classic ECG sign of hypothermia, not of hyperkalemia.

prompt: For stable narrow-complex SVT (per ACLS concepts), initial medication often considered is

options.text: Synchronized cardioversion at 50–100 J as the first step in a stable patient
Amiodarone 300 mg IV push, as used for refractory VF
Adenosine (when vagal maneuvers fail/are inappropriate)
Atropine 1 mg IV to restore normal AV nodal conduction

explanation: Stable SVT algorithms use vagal maneuvers/adenosine; unstable patients may need synchronized cardioversion.

distractorExplanations.b: 300 mg IV push is the cardiac-arrest amiodarone dose, not a first-line treatment for stable SVT.
distractorExplanations.d: Atropine speeds AV conduction and treats bradycardia; it would not terminate re-entrant SVT.

prompt: Synchronized cardioversion is preferred over unsynchronized defibrillation when

options.text: The patient is pulseless with coarse VF and a rapid ventricular rate
The patient has polymorphic VT with a pulse, since synchronizing avoids an R-on-T shock
The patient has stable sinus tachycardia above 150/min from fever
The patient has a pulse with an unstable tachyarrhythmia requiring shock

explanation: Synchronization avoids T-wave shock in organized rhythms with pulses; VF needs defib.

distractorExplanations.b: Polymorphic VT cannot be reliably synchronized, so AHA calls for unsynchronized high-energy shocks.
distractorExplanations.c: Sinus tachycardia is a compensatory rhythm; treat the fever or cause, never cardiovert it.

Scene fibrinolytic therapy as the first choice even when PCI is within 90 minutes
Nitroglycerin and a repeat 12-lead in 30 minutes before choosing a destination

Prominent U waves with flattened T waves and ST depression

options.text: Removing the pads and stopping cardiac monitoring once a pulse returns, since rearrest is rare after sustained ROSC in the field
Ventilating at 20–30 breaths/min to an ETCO2 near 20 mm Hg and accepting an SBP of 70 mm Hg en route
Support ABCs, optimize oxygenation/ventilation carefully, treat hypotension, and consider targeted temperature/PCI indications
Keeping SpO2 at 100% on high-flow oxygen and actively warming the comatose patient above 38 °C to protect the injured brain

prompt: Permissive hypotension in penetrating trauma (select protocols) aims to:

options.text: Avoid popping clots with excessive fluids before surgical hemorrhage control
Raise SBP above 120 mm Hg with large crystalloid boluses before transport
Keep SBP near 80–90 in head injury to lower intracranial pressure
Replace estimated blood loss 3:1 with crystalloid to restore normal vitals on scene

prompt: TXA (tranexamic acid) in trauma is used to:

options.text: Dissolve microvascular clots, as alteplase does in ischemic stroke
Inhibit fibrinolysis and reduce hemorrhage mortality when given early
Reverse warfarin anticoagulation in trauma by replacing clotting factors

prompt: Neurogenic shock features often include

options.text: Hypotension with tachycardia and cool, pale skin below the injury
Hypertension with bradycardia and irregular respirations after head injury
Hypotension with bradycardia and warm dry skin after spinal cord injury
Hypotension with wheezing, urticaria, and flushed skin after an exposure

options.text: Phenytoin loading IV as the first-line drug before any benzodiazepine
Dextrose 50% for every seizing patient before checking the glucose
Haloperidol IM to control the motor activity and agitation

prompt: DKA typically presents with:

options.text: Hyperglycemia, dehydration, and Kussmaul respirations with metabolic acidosis

prompt: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose toxicity may feature
